  7. (a) Show that the momentum of a photon is h/\lambda. [2](b) How many photons of wavelength 500\ \text{nm} does a 1.0\ \text{W} lamp emit per second, assuming all the energy goes into light? [3] [5]
  8. (a) Explain how the photoelectric effect demonstrates the particle nature of light. [3](b) Give two practical applications of photoelectric cells. [2] [5]
Model answers — short (1–4)

1. (a) A photon is the quantum, or smallest indivisible packet, of electromagnetic radiation: light of frequency \nu can be emitted or absorbed only in whole units of energy h\nu. Properties: (i) its energy is E = h\nu = hc/\lambda, fixed entirely by the frequency and independent of the intensity; (ii) it has zero rest mass and always travels at c in vacuum; (iii) it carries momentum p = E/c = h/\lambda even though it has no rest mass; (iv) it is electrically neutral, so it is undeflected by electric and magnetic fields; (v) the intensity of a beam is the number of photons crossing unit area per second, not the energy of each; (vi) in an interaction with an electron, the photon is absorbed whole — it cannot give up part of itself.

(b)

E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{400\times10^{-9}}

E = 4.97\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

E = \frac{4.97\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 3.11\ \text{eV}

2. (a) Laws of photoelectric emission. (i) For a given metal and a given frequency, the number of photoelectrons emitted per second (the photoelectric current) is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident light. (ii) For every metal there is a minimum frequency, the threshold frequency \nu_0, below which no emission occurs however intense the light or however long it shines. (iii) The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons depends only on the frequency of the light and on the metal, and is completely independent of the intensity. (iv) Emission is instantaneous — within about 10^{-9}\ \text{s} of the light arriving — even for very feeble light.

(b) Laws (ii), (iii) and (iv) defeat the wave theory. On the wave picture, light energy arrives spread continuously over the whole surface, and an electron absorbs it gradually. Then: (ii) any frequency should eventually work, provided the light is intense enough or is left on long enough, so there should be no threshold at all; (iii) a more intense wave carries a larger electric field, so it should shake the electrons harder and eject them with more energy — the maximum kinetic energy should depend on intensity, and should not depend on colour; (iv) with very weak light an electron would need minutes or hours to collect enough energy from the spread-out wave, so emission should be delayed, not instantaneous. Experiment contradicts all three. Einstein's resolution is that light arrives as individual photons of energy h\nu, and one electron absorbs one whole photon in a single event.

3. (a) Einstein's photoelectric equation:

h\nu = W + \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}

h\nu is the energy of the single incident photon, which is absorbed completely by one electron. W is the work function of the metal, the least energy needed to free an electron from the surface. \tfrac12mv_{max}^{2} is the maximum kinetic energy with which the electron emerges — it is a maximum because electrons that come from below the surface lose extra energy in collisions on the way out. Using W = h\nu_0, the equation may be written

\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h(\nu-\nu_0)

which shows at once why no emission is possible for \nu < \nu_0: the kinetic energy would have to be negative.

(b) Work function W is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a metal, usually quoted in eV. Threshold frequency \nu_0 = W/h is the lowest frequency of light that can just cause emission, with the electron leaving with zero speed. Threshold wavelength \lambda_0 = hc/W = c/\nu_0 is the corresponding longest wavelength; light of wavelength greater than \lambda_0 can never eject electrons from that metal.

4. (a) The stopping potential V_s is the least negative potential that must be applied to the collecting anode to stop even the fastest photoelectron from reaching it, so that the photoelectric current falls to exactly zero. An electron of charge e moving against a retarding potential V_s loses kinetic energy eV_s. The fastest electron is just stopped when

eV_s = \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}

Substituting this into Einstein's equation h\nu = W + \tfrac12mv_{max}^{2},

h\nu = W + eV_s \;\Rightarrow\; eV_s = h\nu - W

V_s = \frac{h}{e}\nu - \frac{W}{e}

(b) Photon energy at 400\ \text{nm} is 3.11\ \text{eV} (from question 1), so

eV_s = h\nu - W = 3.11 - 2.0 = 1.11\ \text{eV}

V_s = 1.11\ \text{V}

Model answers — short (5–8)

5. (a) From V_s = (h/e)\nu - W/e, a graph of stopping potential against frequency is a straight line. It does not pass through the origin: it meets the \nu-axis at \nu_0 and, if extended backwards, meets the V_s-axis at -W/e. - The slope is h/e. Measuring the slope and multiplying by the known e gives Planck's constant: h = e\times\text{slope}. This is how Millikan measured h in 1916, and it agreed with the value from black-body radiation. - The intercept on the V_s-axis is -W/e, so W = e\times|\text{intercept}|. A striking feature is that the line has the same slope for every metal; changing the metal only shifts the line sideways. That universality is strong evidence that h is a constant of nature, not a property of the material.

(b) The intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency \nu_0 of that metal — the frequency at which the stopping potential is zero, meaning the electrons just barely escape with no kinetic energy. It is related to the work function by W = h\nu_0.

6. (a)

\lambda_0 = \frac{hc}{W} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{2.0\times1.6\times10^{-19}}

\lambda_0 = \frac{1.989\times10^{-25}}{3.2\times10^{-19}} = 6.2\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 622\ \text{nm}

(b) No. The incident wavelength 700\ \text{nm} is greater than the threshold wavelength 622\ \text{nm}, so its frequency is below \nu_0. Checking directly, the photon energy is

E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1.989\times10^{-25}}{700\times10^{-9}} = 2.84\times10^{-19}\ \text{J} = 1.78\ \text{eV}

which is less than the work function 2.0\ \text{eV}. A single photon cannot free an electron, and since an electron absorbs only one photon at a time, no amount of extra intensity and no length of exposure will help — increasing the intensity merely sends more photons, each still too weak.

7. (a) A photon has zero rest mass, so the relativistic energy-momentum relation E^{2} = p^{2}c^{2}+m_0^{2}c^{4} reduces to E = pc. Hence

p = \frac{E}{c} = \frac{h\nu}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda}

(Equivalently, using the equivalent mass m = E/c^{2} = h\nu/c^{2} and p = mc gives the same result.) The existence of this momentum is confirmed by radiation pressure, by the Compton effect and by the tails of comets, which are pushed away from the Sun.

(b) Energy of one photon:

E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1.989\times10^{-25}}{500\times10^{-9}} = 3.98\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

Number emitted per second:

n = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{1.0}{3.98\times10^{-19}} = 2.5\times10^{18}\ \text{s}^{-1}

The number is enormous, which is exactly why the graininess of light is never noticed in everyday life.

8. (a) The photoelectric effect shows three things a wave cannot do. (i) The threshold. If the energy of a wave were spread out, faint red light shining for long enough would accumulate enough energy to free an electron; in fact red light never works on a metal whose threshold lies in the green, however bright. This is only sensible if the energy comes in indivisible lumps of size h\nu, and a single lump must be big enough by itself. (ii) Energy depends on colour, not brightness. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of electrons but leaves their maximum energy exactly unchanged; changing the colour changes the energy. So each electron deals with one photon, and the photon's energy is fixed by \nu. (iii) No time delay. Even at intensities so low that classical theory predicts an hour's wait, the first electrons appear within nanoseconds — because the energy is delivered in a single concentrated event, not gathered gradually. Together these force the picture of light as a stream of particles, each carrying energy h\nu and momentum h/\lambda. (Interference and diffraction equally force the wave picture, and both are true: this is wave-particle duality.)

(b) Applications: (i) in photocells used for automatic street lighting, burglar alarms, automatic doors and counting devices on production lines; (ii) in light meters for photography and in solar cells for electrical power; (iii) in the sound track of film projectors, where the varying light through the track becomes a varying current; (iv) in photomultiplier tubes for detecting very faint light in astronomy and in nuclear particle detectors; (v) in television camera tubes and image intensifiers for night vision.

Long answer / numerical questions [8 marks each]

  1. (a) State the laws of photoelectric emission and explain which of them the wave theory fails to account for. [4](b) Derive Einstein's photoelectric equation and define work function and threshold frequency. [2](c) Light of wavelength 400\ \text{nm} falls on a metal of work function 2.0\ \text{eV}. Find the photon energy in eV, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, the stopping potential and the threshold wavelength. [2] [8] (NEB 2081)
  2. (a) Define stopping potential and show that V_s = (h/e)\nu - W/e. [3](b) Sketch V_s against \nu for two different metals and explain how h and W are found from the graph. [3](c) A metal has \nu_0 = 5.0\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}; find its work function in eV. [2] [8] (NEB 2079 model)
  3. (a) What is a photon? Derive expressions for its energy, equivalent mass and momentum. [4](b) Explain wave-particle duality and state de Broglie's hypothesis. [2](c) A 1.0\ \text{W} source emits light of wavelength 500\ \text{nm}. Find the photon energy and the number of photons emitted per second. [2] [8]
Model answers — long

1. (a) The four laws are as stated in short answer 2(a): current proportional to intensity; a threshold frequency below which nothing happens; maximum kinetic energy determined by frequency alone; and instantaneous emission. The wave theory explains only the first. It fails on the other three. A wave delivers energy continuously and over the whole illuminated area, so (i) there should be no threshold — low-frequency light, made intense enough or left on long enough, should always work; (ii) a more intense wave has a larger amplitude and therefore a larger electric field, so it should give the ejected electrons more kinetic energy, whereas experiment shows the maximum energy is completely independent of intensity and rises only with frequency; (iii) with a very feeble beam an electron would have to collect energy for minutes, so there should be a measurable delay, but none is found.

(b) Derivation. Einstein assumed that light of frequency \nu consists of photons of energy h\nu, and that a photoelectron absorbs one whole photon in a single act. The energy so received is spent in two ways: a minimum amount W must be spent in freeing the electron from the attraction of the metal surface, and whatever remains appears as kinetic energy. For an electron that happens to be right at the surface and loses nothing on the way out, the remainder is a maximum:

h\nu = W + \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}

Work function W is the minimum energy needed to liberate an electron from the metal surface. Threshold frequency \nu_0 is the frequency for which h\nu_0 = W exactly, so the electron just escapes with zero kinetic energy; with W = h\nu_0,

\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h(\nu-\nu_0)

For \nu < \nu_0 the right-hand side is negative, which is impossible — hence no emission at all, at any intensity.

(c)

E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{400\times10^{-9}} = 4.97\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

E = \frac{4.97\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 3.11\ \text{eV}

KE_{max} = E - W = 3.11-2.0 = 1.11\ \text{eV} = 1.77\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

V_s = \frac{KE_{max}}{e} = 1.11\ \text{V}

\lambda_0 = \frac{hc}{W} = \frac{1.989\times10^{-25}}{3.2\times10^{-19}} = 6.2\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 622\ \text{nm}

Check: 622\ \text{nm} > 400\ \text{nm}, so the incident light is indeed energetic enough — consistent with a positive KE_{max}. ✓

2. (a) The stopping potential V_s is the smallest retarding potential difference applied to the anode that reduces the photoelectric current to zero, by turning back even the fastest electron. As an electron of charge e climbs through a retarding potential V_s it loses energy eV_s; the fastest electron is just brought to rest when

eV_s = \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}

Einstein's equation is

h\nu = W + \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = W + eV_s

Rearranging for V_s and dividing throughout by e:

V_s = \frac{h}{e}\nu - \frac{W}{e}

(b) This is of the form y = mx+c, so the graph of V_s against \nu is a straight line of slope h/e and intercept -W/e on the V_s-axis, cutting the \nu-axis at \nu_0 = W/h. For two metals A and B with W_A < W_B, the lines are parallel (same slope h/e), with B's line displaced to the right and its threshold frequency larger. - To find h: measure the slope of either line and multiply by e; h = e\times\text{slope}. - To find W: read the intercept on the V_s axis and multiply by e, W = e\times|{-W/e}|; or read \nu_0 from the \nu-axis and use W = h\nu_0. The fact that both lines have the same slope, whatever the metal, is direct experimental proof that h is a universal constant.

(c)

W = h\nu_0 = 6.63\times10^{-34}\times5.0\times10^{14} = 3.32\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

W = \frac{3.32\times10^{-19}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 2.07\ \text{eV}

3. (a) A photon is the quantum of electromagnetic radiation — the smallest indivisible packet in which light of a given frequency can be emitted or absorbed. Energy. Planck's hypothesis, which Einstein extended to free radiation, gives

E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}

Equivalent mass. A photon has zero rest mass, but it carries energy, and by Einstein's mass-energy relation E = mc^{2} this energy is equivalent to a mass

m = \frac{E}{c^{2}} = \frac{h\nu}{c^{2}} = \frac{h}{\lambda c}

This is the mass that makes light bend in a gravitational field. Momentum. Since the photon travels at c,

p = mc = \frac{h\nu}{c^{2}}\cdot c = \frac{h\nu}{c} = \frac{h}{\lambda}

The same result follows from the relativistic relation E = pc for a massless particle. Photon momentum is real and measurable: it produces radiation pressure, drives comet tails away from the Sun, and shows up quantitatively in the Compton effect.

(b) Wave-particle duality is the principle that radiation and matter both show wave behaviour in some experiments and particle behaviour in others, and that neither picture alone is complete. Light diffracts and interferes (Young's slits, gratings, thin films) — purely wave behaviour; yet it shows a photoelectric threshold and Compton scattering — purely particle behaviour. The two never appear in the same measurement, so there is no contradiction; which face shows depends on what you ask of the light. de Broglie's hypothesis extends the symmetry to matter: every moving particle has an associated wave of wavelength

\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}

For everyday objects \lambda is unimaginably small (10^{-34}\ \text{m} for a cricket ball) and no wave effect is seen, but for an electron accelerated through 100\ \text{V} it is about 1.2\times10^{-10}\ \text{m} — comparable with atomic spacings, which is why electrons are diffracted by crystals (Davisson and Germer) and why the electron microscope works.

(c)

E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{500\times10^{-9}} = 3.98\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}

E = 2.49\ \text{eV}

n = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{1.0}{3.98\times10^{-19}} = 2.5\times10^{18}\ \text{photons per second}

Einstein's photoelectric equation

We want a relation between the colour of the light, the metal, and the speed of the fastest electron that comes off.

Setting up. Light of frequency \nu falls on a clean metal surface in a vacuum. Einstein made two assumptions: that the light arrives as separate photons, each carrying energy h\nu; and that one photoelectron absorbs one complete photon, never a part of one and never two at once.

Step 1 — write the energy the electron receives. The whole photon is absorbed, so the electron gains

E_{in} = h\nu

Step 2 — subtract the price of escaping. An electron inside the metal is held there by the attraction of the positive ions. The least energy that any electron must pay to get out through the surface is the work function W. So the energy left over is

E_{left} = h\nu - W

Step 3 — recognise that most electrons pay more than the minimum. An electron starting below the surface loses extra energy in collisions on its way out, so it emerges with less than E_{left}. Only an electron right at the surface, losing nothing on the way, keeps all of it. That electron is the fastest one:

\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h\nu - W

Step 4 — write it in the standard form. Move W to the other side:

h\nu = W + \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}

Step 5 — express the work function as a frequency. Define the threshold frequency \nu_0 as the frequency of the photon whose energy is exactly W:

W = h\nu_0

Step 6 — substitute this into Step 3.

\frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2} = h\nu - h\nu_0 = h(\nu-\nu_0)

Step 7 — connect to the stopping potential. The fastest electron is just turned back by a retarding potential V_s when the work done against it equals that kinetic energy:

eV_s = h\nu - W

Step 8 — divide by e to get a straight-line form.

V_s = \frac{h}{e}\nu - \frac{W}{e}

Result.

h\nu = W + \frac{1}{2}mv_{max}^{2}, \qquad V_s = \frac{h}{e}\nu - \frac{W}{e}

What it means. Every puzzling feature of photoelectric emission drops out of this one line. If \nu < \nu_0 the right-hand side of Step 6 is negative, which is impossible for a kinetic energy, so no electrons come off at all — that is the threshold. Making the light brighter sends more photons, so more electrons are released and the current grows, but each photon still carries the same h\nu, so the maximum kinetic energy does not change. The energy arrives in one concentrated event rather than being gathered slowly, so emission is instantaneous. And the graph of V_s against \nu must be a straight line of slope h/e, the same for every metal — which is how Planck's constant was measured from a photocell.

Conditions. The surface must be clean and in a vacuum, since a layer of oxide or grease changes W; the equation is non-relativistic, so it fails for very energetic photons; and it assumes single-photon absorption, which breaks down only at laser intensities, where two-photon processes become possible.

Examiner's note — Photons

Convert to electronvolts early and stay there: E(\text{eV}) = 1242/\lambda(\text{nm}) is worth memorising as a check, and it makes KE_{max} = E - W a one-line subtraction. Always say that one electron absorbs one whole photon — that single sentence is what makes the threshold and the instantaneous emission intelligible, and examiners look for it. Keep the three "independent of intensity" facts separate from the one fact that is proportional to intensity (the current). In graph questions, label the slope h/e and the intercepts -W/e and \nu_0, and remember that lines for different metals are parallel.

3.22 Semiconductor devices

CDC allots 6 teaching hours. Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, the p-n junction and its biasing, half-wave and full-wave rectification, the transistor and its characteristics and gain, and the basic logic gates are all examinable; this unit supplies a Group C question most years.

Short answer questions [5 marks each]

  1. (a) Distinguish between conductors, semiconductors and insulators using energy-band diagrams. [3](b) Why does the resistance of a semiconductor fall as temperature rises? [2] [5] (NEB 2080)

  5. (a) Explain half-wave rectification with a circuit diagram and output waveform. [3](b) Why is full-wave rectification preferred? [2] [5] (NEB 2079 model)

  8. (a) Define \alpha and \beta for a transistor and show that \beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha). [3](b) A transistor has \beta = 100 and I_B = 50\ \mu\text{A}; find I_C, I_E and \alpha. [2] [5]
  9. (a) Draw the symbols and truth tables of the OR, AND and NOT gates. [3](b) Show that a NAND gate followed by a NOT gate gives an AND gate. [2] [5]
Model answers — short (1–5)

1. (a) In a solid the allowed electron energies form bands. The highest band that is full at absolute zero is the valence band; the next empty one is the conduction band; the gap between them is the forbidden energy gap E_g. - Conductor: the valence and conduction bands overlap (or the valence band is only half full), so E_g = 0. Electrons can move into unoccupied levels under the smallest field, and conductivity is very high. Example: copper. - Semiconductor: the bands are separated by a small gap, about 1.1\ \text{eV} in silicon and 0.72\ \text{eV} in germanium. At 0\ \text{K} it is an insulator, but at room temperature thermal energy lifts a few electrons across, leaving holes behind, so it conducts feebly. - Insulator: the gap is large, 5\ \text{eV} or more (diamond \approx6\ \text{eV}). Thermal energy at room temperature (\approx0.026\ \text{eV}) cannot lift electrons across, so the conduction band stays empty and no current flows.

(b) A metal has a fixed number of free electrons; heating it only increases the lattice vibrations, which scatter the electrons more, so its resistance rises. A semiconductor is different: at higher temperature many more electron-hole pairs are created by thermal excitation across the small gap, so the number of charge carriers n increases exponentially. This gain in carrier number far outweighs the loss in mobility due to increased scattering, so the conductivity rises and the resistance falls. Semiconductors therefore have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance — the basis of the thermistor.

2. (a) An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure specimen — pure silicon or germanium with no added impurity. Its conduction is due entirely to thermally generated electron-hole pairs, so n_e = n_h, and its conductivity is small and depends only on temperature. An extrinsic semiconductor has a controlled impurity deliberately added ("doping"), typically one atom in 10^{6}–10^{8}. Its conductivity is far higher, is dominated by one type of carrier, and can be set by the doping level.

(b) n-type: a pentavalent impurity (arsenic, antimony, phosphorus) is added to tetravalent silicon. Four of its five valence electrons form covalent bonds with neighbours; the fifth is left over, only loosely bound, and is freed by a tiny amount of energy (\approx0.01\ \text{eV}). The impurity is called a donor. Majority carriers: electrons; minority carriers: holes. p-type: a trivalent impurity (boron, indium, gallium, aluminium) is added. It can form only three covalent bonds, so one bond is left incomplete — a hole, which readily accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, so the hole moves. The impurity is called an acceptor. Majority carriers: holes; minority carriers: electrons. Both types remain electrically neutral overall: an n-type crystal has extra free electrons but an equal number of fixed positive donor ions.

3. (a) When p-type and n-type materials are joined, there is a very large concentration difference across the junction: many electrons on the n-side and many holes on the p-side. So electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, and they recombine near the junction. Each electron that leaves the n-side exposes a fixed positive donor ion, and each hole that leaves the p-side exposes a fixed negative acceptor ion. A narrow region on either side of the junction is thus stripped of mobile carriers and contains only these immobile charged ions; this is the depletion layer, about 10^{-6}\ \text{m} wide. The exposed ions set up an electric field pointing from the n-side to the p-side, which opposes further diffusion. Equilibrium is reached when this field just stops the net diffusion. The potential difference across the layer is the potential barrier, about 0.3\ \text{V} for germanium and 0.7\ \text{V} for silicon. No external current flows, because the barrier blocks it.

(b) Forward bias (p to +, n to -): the applied field opposes the internal field, so majority carriers are pushed towards the junction, they neutralise some of the exposed ions, and the depletion layer becomes narrower and the barrier lower. Beyond the knee voltage the barrier is essentially cancelled and a large current flows; the resistance is low (a few ohms). Reverse bias (p to -, n to +): the applied field adds to the internal field, majority carriers are pulled away from the junction, more ions are exposed, and the depletion layer becomes wider and the barrier higher. Only a tiny leakage current due to minority carriers (a few \mu\text{A}) flows; the resistance is very high (megohms).

4. (a) The characteristic is plotted with V on the x-axis and I on the y-axis, with reverse values in the third quadrant. Forward branch (first quadrant): almost no current until the applied voltage reaches the knee voltage (0.7\ \text{V} for Si, 0.3\ \text{V} for Ge), after which the current rises very steeply and almost vertically; the graph is markedly non-linear, so the diode does not obey Ohm's law. Reverse branch (third quadrant): a very small, almost constant reverse saturation current of a few microamperes, independent of voltage, until at the breakdown voltage the reverse current suddenly becomes very large.

(b) Knee (cut-in or threshold) voltage is the forward voltage at which the diode current begins to increase rapidly, because the applied voltage has just overcome the potential barrier. Breakdown voltage is the reverse voltage at which the reverse current increases abruptly and without limit, because the strong field either tears electrons out of covalent bonds (Zener breakdown) or accelerates minority carriers enough to ionise atoms in a chain reaction (avalanche breakdown). An ordinary diode is destroyed if the current is not limited; a Zener diode is designed to work there and is used as a voltage regulator.

5. (a) In half-wave rectification a single diode is joined in series with the load resistance R_L across the secondary of a transformer. During the half cycle in which the secondary makes the diode's p-side positive, the diode is forward biased, its resistance is low, and current flows through R_L, giving an output voltage that follows the input. During the next half cycle the polarity reverses, the diode is reverse biased, its resistance is enormous, and virtually no current flows, so the output is zero. The output is therefore a series of unidirectional pulses with gaps between them — direct current, but only for half the time (see Figure 19, top).

(b) Full-wave rectification is preferred because: (i) it uses both halves of the input, so its efficiency is about 81\% against 40.6\% for half-wave; (ii) the output has no gaps, so the ripple factor is much lower (0.48 against 1.21 for half-wave), so the output is far easier to smooth with a filter; (iii) the ripple frequency is doubled (100\ \text{Hz} from a 50\ \text{Hz} mains), and a higher ripple frequency is easier to filter out; (iv) the d.c. output voltage is twice as large for the same peak.

Model answers — short (6–9)

6. (a) In the centre-tapped arrangement, the secondary of the transformer has a tapping at its mid-point, which is earthed and joined to one end of the load. The two ends of the secondary are connected to the p-sides of two diodes D_1 and D_2, and their n-sides are joined together to the other end of the load. Because the tapping is at the centre, the two halves of the secondary are always of opposite polarity relative to it. During the first half cycle, end A is positive with respect to the tap, so D_1 is forward biased and conducts while D_2 is reverse biased and blocks; current flows through R_L in one direction. During the second half cycle, end B is positive, so D_2 conducts and D_1 blocks; the current again flows through R_L in the same direction, because the two diodes feed the load from the same side. Both halves of the input therefore give output, and the waveform is a continuous train of humps (Figure 19, bottom).

(b) In half-wave rectification, the output has one pulse per input cycle, so the ripple frequency equals the input frequency:

f_{ripple} = 50\ \text{Hz}

In full-wave rectification, both halves of each input cycle produce a pulse, so there are two pulses per cycle:

f_{ripple} = 2\times50 = 100\ \text{Hz}

7. (a) An n-p-n transistor is a single crystal with three doped regions. The emitter is heavily doped and of moderate size; it emits the majority carriers (electrons) into the device. The base is the thin middle p-region, very thin (10^{-6}\ \text{m}) and lightly doped; it controls the flow. The collector is an n-region, moderately doped but physically the largest, and it collects the carriers. In normal operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased. Why the base is thin and lightly doped: electrons injected from the emitter into the base are minority carriers there and would be lost by recombination with holes. If the base were thick or heavily doped, most of them would recombine and never reach the collector, so the transistor would not amplify. Because it is thin and lightly doped, only about 2–5\% of the electrons recombine (giving the small base current I_B) and 95–98\% diffuse right across and are swept into the collector by its reverse-biased field. It is this near-total transfer that gives a large current gain.

(b) The emitter current divides between the base and the collector, so by conservation of charge at the transistor:

I_E = I_B + I_C

with I_B only a few per cent of I_E, so I_C \approx I_E.

8. (a) Common-base current gain \alpha is the ratio of the collector current to the emitter current:

\alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E}

It is a little less than 1, typically 0.95–0.99. Common-emitter current gain \beta is the ratio of the collector current to the base current:

\beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B}

and is large, typically 20–500. Relation. Start from I_E = I_B+I_C, and divide every term by I_C:

\frac{I_E}{I_C} = \frac{I_B}{I_C}+1

\frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\beta}+1 = \frac{1+\beta}{\beta}

Inverting, \alpha = \beta/(1+\beta). Solving instead for \beta: \beta\alpha = \beta - \alpha\beta... more directly, from \alpha(1+\beta) = \beta we get \alpha = \beta-\alpha\beta, so \alpha = \beta(1-\alpha) and

\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}

(b)

I_C = \beta I_B = 100\times50\times10^{-6} = 5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 5.0\ \text{mA}

I_E = I_B+I_C = 0.05+5.0 = 5.05\ \text{mA}

\alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E} = \frac{5.00}{5.05} = 0.990

Check: \beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha) = 0.990/0.0099 = 100. ✓

9. (a)

Gate Symbol Boolean Truth table (A,B \to Y)
OR flat back, curved front, two inputs Y = A+B 00\to0; 01\to1; 10\to1; 11\to1
AND flat back, D-shaped front Y = A\cdot B 00\to0; 01\to0; 10\to0; 11\to1
NOT triangle with a small circle at the tip Y = \bar{A} 0\to1; 1\to0

The OR gate gives output 1 if any input is 1; the AND gate only if all inputs are 1; the NOT gate (inverter) reverses whatever it is given.

(b) A NAND gate gives Y_1 = \overline{A\cdot B} — the AND output inverted. Feeding this into a NOT gate inverts it once more:

Y = \overline{Y_1} = \overline{\overline{A\cdot B}} = A\cdot B

because inverting twice restores the original (involution law). The truth table confirms it: for A,B = 0,0, NAND gives 1 and NOT gives 0; for 0,1 and 1,0, NAND gives 1 and NOT gives 0; for 1,1, NAND gives 0 and NOT gives 1. Output is 1 only when both inputs are 1 — an AND gate. (Since a NOT gate can itself be made by tying the two inputs of a NAND together, the NAND gate is a universal gate.)

Model answers — long

1. (a) In a crystal the allowed energies form bands separated by forbidden gaps. The band filled at 0\ \text{K} is the valence band, the empty one above it the conduction band, and their separation is the energy gap E_g. Conduction requires electrons with empty levels close above them to move into. Conductor: the two bands overlap, E_g = 0; countless empty levels lie immediately above the occupied ones, so even a very weak field produces a large current. Resistivity 10^{-8}–10^{-6}\ \Omega\,\text{m}; resistance increases with temperature. Semiconductor: E_g is small, 1.1\ \text{eV} (Si) or 0.72\ \text{eV} (Ge). At 0\ \text{K} the conduction band is empty and the crystal is an insulator, but at 300\ \text{K} thermal energy promotes a few electrons across, each leaving a hole behind; both carry current. Resistivity 10^{-5}–10^{4}\ \Omega\,\text{m}; resistance decreases with temperature. Insulator: E_g is large, 5–10\ \text{eV}. Room-temperature thermal energy is only about 0.026\ \text{eV}, hopelessly small, so the conduction band stays empty. Resistivity 10^{11}–10^{19}\ \Omega\,\text{m}.

(b) Doping. Adding a pentavalent atom (As, Sb, P) to silicon gives one spare electron per impurity atom, loosely bound and easily freed: an n-type crystal, majority carriers electrons, impurity called a donor. Adding a trivalent atom (B, In, Ga) leaves one covalent bond incomplete, a hole that can accept an electron: a p-type crystal, majority carriers holes, impurity called an acceptor. Both remain electrically neutral overall. Depletion layer. Joining the two, electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, driven by the concentration difference, and recombine near the boundary. This leaves behind immobile positive donor ions on the n-side and negative acceptor ions on the p-side, in a narrow region with almost no mobile carriers — the depletion layer, roughly 1\ \mu\text{m} wide. These fixed ions create an internal field from n to p, which opposes further diffusion, and the associated potential difference is the potential barrier (0.7\ \text{V} for Si, 0.3\ \text{V} for Ge). At equilibrium diffusion stops and no net current flows.

(c) Forward characteristic (first quadrant): current is negligible up to the knee voltage (0.7\ \text{V} for Si), then rises almost vertically; the curve is non-linear, so the diode disobeys Ohm's law and its dynamic resistance falls with current. Reverse characteristic (third quadrant): only a tiny reverse saturation current of a few \mu\text{A}, nearly independent of voltage, until at the breakdown voltage the current increases abruptly. Both points must be labelled on the sketch.

2. (a) Half-wave. A single diode is in series with R_L across the transformer secondary. On the half cycle that forward-biases the diode, current flows and the output follows the input; on the other half the diode blocks and the output is zero. The output is a train of pulses separated by gaps (Figure 19, top). Full-wave (centre-tapped). The secondary has an earthed centre tap joined to one end of the load; the two ends feed diodes D_1 and D_2, whose other terminals join at the far end of the load. The two halves of the secondary are always of opposite polarity with respect to the tap, so on the first half cycle D_1 conducts and D_2 blocks, and on the second half cycle D_2 conducts and D_1 blocks. In both cases the current passes through R_L in the same direction, so the negative halves are effectively flipped up and the output is a continuous series of humps (Figure 19, bottom). (A bridge of four diodes does the same job without a centre tap.)

(b)

Half-wave Full-wave
Diodes 1 2 (centre-tap) or 4 (bridge)
Fraction of input used half all
Maximum efficiency 40.6\% 81.2\%
Ripple factor 1.21 0.48
Ripple frequency (for f input) f 2f
D.C. output V_0/\pi 2V_0/\pi

(c) For a 50\ \text{Hz} supply, the half-wave ripple frequency is 50\ \text{Hz} (one pulse per cycle) and the full-wave ripple frequency is 100\ \text{Hz} (two pulses per cycle). Why a capacitor is connected across the load. The rectified output is unidirectional but far from steady; the fluctuation is the ripple. A large capacitor in parallel with R_L acts as a reservoir: it charges up almost to the peak voltage while the output is rising, and then, while the rectified voltage falls towards zero, it discharges slowly through R_L (time constant CR_L made much longer than the ripple period). The output therefore sags only a little between peaks, and the ripple is greatly reduced. Its reactance X_C = 1/2\pi fC is small for the a.c. ripple component, which it short-circuits, but infinite for the d.c. component, which it passes on to the load — so it is a simple low-pass filter. This works better in the full-wave case because the gaps are shorter and the ripple frequency twice as high.

3. (a) An n-p-n transistor consists of a thin p-type base sandwiched between a heavily doped n-type emitter and a moderately doped, physically larger n-type collector. In normal amplifying operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction is reverse biased. Working. The forward bias on the emitter junction is easily overcome, so the heavily doped emitter injects a large stream of electrons into the base. In the base these electrons are minority carriers and could recombine with holes, but the base is very thin and lightly doped, so only about 2–5\% of them do; these constitute the small base current I_B. The remaining 95–98\% diffuse right across the base and reach the edge of the reverse-biased collector junction, where the strong field there sweeps them straight into the collector, giving I_C. Thus I_E = I_B+I_C with I_C \approx I_E. Why the base is thin and lightly doped: to keep recombination small so that nearly all the emitted carriers reach the collector. A thick or heavily doped base would lose most of them, \alpha would fall well below 1, and \beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha) would collapse — there would be no useful amplification. The amplification itself comes from transferring a current from a low-resistance input circuit (forward-biased junction) to a high-resistance output circuit (reverse-biased junction) at nearly the same size, so that the voltage and power are greatly increased. ("Transistor" = transfer + resistor.)

(b) \alpha = I_C/I_E (common base), \beta = I_C/I_B (common emitter). From I_E = I_B + I_C, divide by I_C:

\frac{I_E}{I_C} = \frac{I_B}{I_C} + 1

\frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{\beta} + 1 = \frac{1+\beta}{\beta}

\alpha = \frac{\beta}{1+\beta}

Rearranging this for \beta: \alpha(1+\beta) = \beta, so \alpha = \beta(1-\alpha) and

\beta = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}

Since \alpha is just below 1, the denominator 1-\alpha is tiny and \beta is large — that is why a 1\% change in \alpha makes an enormous difference to the gain.

(c)

I_C = \beta I_B = 100\times50\ \mu\text{A} = 5.0\ \text{mA}

I_E = I_B+I_C = 0.05+5.0 = 5.05\ \text{mA}

\alpha = \frac{I_C}{I_E} = \frac{5.00}{5.05} = 0.990

A_V = \beta\times\frac{R_{out}}{R_{in}} = 100\times\frac{5.0\times10^{3}}{1.0\times10^{3}} = 500

Check: \beta = \alpha/(1-\alpha) = 0.990/0.010 = 100. ✓ A voltage gain of 500 from a current gain of 100 shows how the resistance ratio does the rest of the work.

Examiner's note — Semiconductor devices

Band diagrams must show three things: the valence band, the conduction band and the size of the gap — and the gap values 1.1\ \text{eV} (Si) and 0.72\ \text{eV} (Ge) are worth quoting. Never say a doped crystal is charged: n-type has extra free electrons but an equal number of fixed positive ions, so it is neutral. In rectifier questions the waveform sketch carries marks of its own — draw the input and output on the same time axis and label the ripple frequency. For the \alpha–\beta derivation, start from I_E = I_B+I_C and divide by I_C; that is the whole proof. And in transistor numericals, remember that I_B is in microamperes while I_C is in milliamperes — mixing them up is the single most common error in this unit.

3.23 Quantization of energy

CDC allots 8 teaching hours — the largest single unit in the Grade 12 course. Bohr's theory of the hydrogen atom, the radius and energy of the orbits, the spectral series, energy-level diagrams, excitation and ionisation, de Broglie waves and the production and properties of X-rays are all examinable, and something from this unit appears in Group C almost every year.

Model answers — short (1–5)

1. (a) Postulate 1 (stationary orbits). The electron revolves round the nucleus only in certain allowed circular orbits, called stationary orbits, in which the necessary centripetal force is supplied by the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus. Postulate 2 (quantisation of angular momentum). Only those orbits are allowed for which the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2\pi:

mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}, \qquad n = 1,2,3,\ldots

Postulate 3 (no radiation in a stationary orbit). While the electron remains in such an orbit it does not radiate energy, however fast it accelerates. Postulate 4 (frequency condition). Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between two allowed orbits, and the photon frequency is fixed by the energy difference:

h\nu = E_2 - E_1

(b) Rutherford's model had two fatal defects. (i) Instability. A circling electron is accelerating, and classical electromagnetism says an accelerating charge must radiate; it would lose energy continuously, spiral inwards and hit the nucleus in about 10^{-8}\ \text{s}. Every atom would collapse. Postulate 3 removes this by simply forbidding radiation from an allowed orbit; postulates 1 and 2 provide a smallest orbit (n = 1) below which the electron cannot fall. (ii) Continuous spectrum. As the electron spiralled in, its frequency of revolution would change continuously, so the atom would emit a continuous band of all frequencies. In fact hydrogen emits a line spectrum of sharp, definite wavelengths. Postulate 4 explains this: only certain energy differences exist, so only certain photon frequencies can be emitted.

2. (a) Let an electron of mass m and charge e move with speed v in a circular orbit of radius r about a nucleus of charge +e (hydrogen). The electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force:

\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}

mv^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Bohr's quantisation condition gives mvr = nh/2\pi, so v = nh/2\pi mr. Substituting,

m\left(\frac{nh}{2\pi mr}\right)^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

\frac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mr^{2}} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Multiplying both sides by r^{2} and rearranging,

r_n = \frac{\varepsilon_0n^{2}h^{2}}{\pi me^{2}}

(b) Everything in that expression except n is a constant of nature, so

r_n \propto n^{2}

The orbits are not equally spaced: they get rapidly further apart. With r_1 = 0.53\ \text{Å},

r_2 = 2^{2}\times0.53 = 2.12\ \text{Å} = 2.12\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}

3. (a) The electron has both kinetic and potential energy. Kinetic energy. From the force equation mv^{2} = e^{2}/4\pi\varepsilon_0r,

KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Potential energy. For charges +e and -e a distance r apart, taking the zero at infinity,

PE = -\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Total energy.

E = KE+PE = \frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r}-\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r} = -\frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0r}

Substituting r_n = \varepsilon_0n^{2}h^{2}/\pi me^{2},

E_n = -\frac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}

(b) The energy is negative because the zero of potential energy is fixed at infinite separation, where the electron is free and at rest. A bound electron has less energy than that, so its total energy must be below zero. Physically the negative sign means the electron is trapped: an amount of energy +13.6/n^{2}\ \text{eV} must be supplied from outside to pull it away from the nucleus altogether. Note also that |PE| = 2\times KE, and E = -KE, which is the virial theorem for an inverse-square force.

4. (a) The levels are drawn as horizontal lines at E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\ \text{eV}: -13.6 for n=1, -3.40 for n=2, -1.51 for n=3, -0.85 for n=4, -0.54 for n=5, and 0 for n = \infty. The lines crowd together as n increases (Figure 20). Downward arrows show the emission series: - Lyman series: all transitions ending on n = 1. - Balmer series: all transitions ending on n = 2. - Paschen series: all transitions ending on n = 3. (Brackett ends on n=4 and Pfund on n=5.)

(b) The Lyman transitions have the largest energy differences (up to 13.6\ \text{eV}), so they lie in the ultraviolet. The Balmer transitions lie in the visible region (and the near ultraviolet at the series limit) — these are the four lines actually seen in a hydrogen discharge tube, red 656\ \text{nm}, blue-green 486\ \text{nm}, violet 434\ \text{nm} and 410\ \text{nm}. Paschen, Brackett and Pfund lie in the infrared, progressively further into it.

5. (a) Excitation energy is the energy that must be supplied to lift an electron from the ground state to a higher (excited) level; the first excitation energy of hydrogen is E_2-E_1. Excitation potential is the accelerating potential difference in volts through which an electron must fall to acquire that energy — numerically equal to the excitation energy in eV. Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove the electron completely from the atom, that is to raise it from the ground state to n = \infty. Ionisation potential is the corresponding potential difference in volts.

(b)

E_{ion} = E_\infty - E_1 = 0-(-13.6) = 13.6\ \text{eV}

so the ionisation potential is 13.6\ \text{V}.

E_{exc,1} = E_2-E_1 = -3.40-(-13.6) = 10.2\ \text{eV}

so the first excitation potential is 10.2\ \text{V}. (These are the numbers confirmed directly by the Franck-Hertz experiment.)

Model answers — short (6–10)

6. (a) The Balmer series ends on n_f = 2, and the first line is the transition from n_i = 3. Rydberg's formula gives

\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right) = R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right)

\frac{1}{\lambda} = 1.097\times10^{7}\times\frac{5}{36} = 1.524\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}

\lambda = \frac{1}{1.524\times10^{6}} = 6.56\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 656\ \text{nm}

(b) It lies in the visible region, at the red end; it is the bright red line known as H_\alpha, the most conspicuous line in the hydrogen spectrum and a familiar feature of the spectra of stars and nebulae. Check by energy: E_3-E_2 = -1.51-(-3.40) = 1.89\ \text{eV}, and \lambda = 1242/1.89 = 657\ \text{nm}. ✓

7. (a) de Broglie's hypothesis: just as light, long regarded as a wave, behaves in some experiments as a stream of particles, so every moving material particle has a wave associated with it. The wavelength is

\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}

For a 1\ \text{kg} body moving at 1\ \text{m s}^{-1} this is 6.6\times10^{-34}\ \text{m} — undetectable. For an electron accelerated through 100\ \text{V} it is 1.2\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}, comparable with the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is why electrons are diffracted by crystals.

(b) De Broglie argued that a stationary orbit is one in which the electron wave joins smoothly onto itself after going once round — a standing wave on a circle. If it did not, successive circuits would interfere destructively and the wave would cancel itself out. The condition for the wave to close up is that the circumference contains a whole number of wavelengths:

2\pi r = n\lambda

Substituting \lambda = h/mv,

2\pi r = \frac{nh}{mv}

mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}

which is exactly Bohr's quantisation condition. What Bohr had to assume, de Broglie explained: the integer n is simply the number of wavelengths that fit round the orbit.

8. (a) In a Coolidge tube, a tungsten filament in a highly evacuated tube is heated by a low-voltage supply and emits electrons by thermionic emission; the filament current controls how many, and hence the intensity of the X-rays. These electrons are accelerated through a very high potential difference (tens of kilovolts) towards a target of a high-melting-point, high-atomic-number metal such as tungsten or molybdenum, set at an angle in a massive copper anode. On striking the target the electrons are suddenly stopped; less than 1\% of their kinetic energy is converted into X-rays and the rest into heat, so the anode must be cooled by circulating oil or water or by rotating it. The quality (penetrating power) of the X-rays is controlled by the accelerating voltage, the intensity by the filament current.

(b) An electron accelerated through V arrives with kinetic energy eV. In the most extreme possible event, the electron is brought to rest in a single collision and all of its energy goes into one photon. That photon has the greatest possible energy, and so the shortest possible wavelength:

eV = h\nu_{max} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}} \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}

\lambda_{min} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times50\times10^{3}} = 2.49\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}

This is the Duane-Hunt limit; note it depends only on V, not on the target material.

9. (a) The continuous spectrum (bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation) arises from electrons that are decelerated in the field of the target nuclei, losing an arbitrary fraction of their energy in each event. It is therefore a smooth, continuous distribution of all wavelengths above a sharp minimum \lambda_{min} = hc/eV, and it depends only on the accelerating voltage, not on the target material. The characteristic spectrum is a set of sharp, intense lines (the K, L, M series) superposed on the continuous background. It arises when an incident electron knocks an electron out of an inner shell of a target atom; an electron from a higher shell then falls into the vacancy and emits a photon whose energy is the difference between two well-defined atomic levels. These wavelengths depend only on the target material, not on the voltage — though the voltage must exceed a threshold before the lines appear at all. (Moseley's law relates their frequencies to the atomic number, which is how Z was first measured.)

(b) Properties: (i) they are electromagnetic waves of very short wavelength (10^{-8} to 10^{-13}\ \text{m}), travelling at c; (ii) they are uncharged, so they are undeflected by electric and magnetic fields; (iii) they are highly penetrating, passing through flesh, wood and thin metal, and absorption increases sharply with the atomic number and thickness of the absorber; (iv) they ionise gases, affect photographic plates, cause fluorescence, and can be diffracted by crystals, which proves they are waves; (v) they damage living tissue. Uses: medical radiography of bones and teeth; radiotherapy for cancer; detection of flaws and cracks in castings and welds; airport and customs security scanning; X-ray crystallography, which determines the structure of crystals and of molecules such as DNA.

10. (a) Limitations of Bohr's theory. (i) It works only for hydrogen and hydrogen-like one-electron ions (\text{He}^{+}, \text{Li}^{2+}); it fails completely for any atom with two or more electrons, because it cannot handle the repulsion between them. (ii) It cannot explain the fine structure of spectral lines — lines that a good spectrometer resolves into two or more closely spaced components. (iii) It cannot explain the relative intensities of lines, or why some transitions are much more probable than others. (iv) It cannot explain the Zeeman and Stark effects, the splitting of lines in magnetic and electric fields. (v) It is a hybrid: it uses classical mechanics for the orbit but arbitrarily forbids classical radiation, without saying why. (vi) It assumes a definite orbit of definite radius and speed, which violates the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

(b) Because helium has two electrons. Bohr's calculation is built on a single electron moving under a single inverse-square force from the nucleus, and the whole derivation of r_n and E_n depends on that one force. In helium each electron is attracted by the nucleus and repelled by the other electron, whose position is itself changing. This is a three-body problem with no exact solution, and the repulsion term cannot be written in a form that allows a simple quantisation condition. The predicted energy levels come out badly wrong. The correct treatment came only with the wave mechanics of Schrödinger, in which the electron is described by a probability cloud rather than an orbit.

1. (a) The four postulates are as listed in short answer 1(a): circular stationary orbits held by electrostatic attraction; angular momentum quantised as mvr = nh/2\pi; no radiation while in a stationary orbit; and radiation only on a jump, with h\nu = E_2-E_1.

(b) See the derivation box below for the step-by-step argument. The results are

r_n = \frac{\varepsilon_0n^{2}h^{2}}{\pi me^{2}} = 0.53\,n^{2}\ \text{Å}

E_n = -\frac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}

Both follow from just two equations — the force equation e^{2}/4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{2} = mv^{2}/r and the quantisation condition mvr = nh/2\pi — solved simultaneously for r and then for E = KE+PE.

(c)

r_2 = n^{2}r_1 = 4\times0.53 = 2.12\ \text{Å} = 2.12\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}

E_3 = \frac{E_1}{n^{2}} = \frac{-13.6}{9} = -1.51\ \text{eV}

Check: the energy needed to ionise an atom already in the third level is only 1.51\ \text{eV}, far less than the 13.6\ \text{eV} from the ground state — excited atoms are much easier to ionise, as they must be. ✓

2. (a) The allowed energies are E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\ \text{eV}, so the levels are drawn as horizontal lines at -13.6, -3.40, -1.51, -0.85, -0.54\ \text{eV} and so on up to 0 at n = \infty (Figure 20). Because E_n goes as 1/n^{2}, the spacing shrinks rapidly and the levels crowd together as they approach the ionisation limit. Every emission line corresponds to a downward jump between two of these levels, with h\nu = E_i - E_f; because the levels are discrete, only certain photon energies are possible, which is why the spectrum consists of sharp lines. Grouping the transitions by their final level explains the series at once: - transitions ending on n = 1 have the largest energy gaps (from 10.2 up to 13.6\ \text{eV}) and form the Lyman series in the ultraviolet; - transitions ending on n = 2 have gaps of 1.89 to 3.40\ \text{eV}, corresponding to 656 down to 365\ \text{nm}, so they form the Balmer series in the visible; - transitions ending on n = 3 have still smaller gaps and form the Paschen series in the infrared, with Brackett (n=4) and Pfund (n=5) further into the infrared. In general 1/\lambda = R\left(1/n_f^{2}-1/n_i^{2}\right).

(b) Excitation energy is the energy needed to raise the electron from the ground state to a specified higher level; ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove it entirely, to n = \infty.

E_{exc,1} = E_2-E_1 = -3.40+13.6 = 10.2\ \text{eV}

E_{exc,2} = E_3-E_1 = -1.51+13.6 = 12.1\ \text{eV}

E_{ion} = 0-(-13.6) = 13.6\ \text{eV}

so the first excitation potential is 10.2\ \text{V} and the ionisation potential 13.6\ \text{V}.

(c) First Balmer line (n_i = 3 \to n_f = 2):

\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) = 1.097\times10^{7}\times0.1389 = 1.524\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}

\lambda = 6.56\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 656\ \text{nm} \quad(\text{red, visible})

Lyman series limit (n_i = \infty \to n_f = 1):

\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{1}-0\right) = 1.097\times10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}

\lambda = 9.12\times10^{-8}\ \text{m} = 91.2\ \text{nm} \quad(\text{far ultraviolet})

Check: the Lyman limit corresponds to 1242/91.2 = 13.6\ \text{eV}, exactly the ionisation energy — as it must, since the series limit is the transition from a just-free electron to the ground state. ✓

3. (a) Coolidge tube. A tungsten filament, heated by a separate low-voltage supply inside a highly evacuated glass tube, emits electrons thermionically. These are focused by a molybdenum cup and accelerated through a potential difference of 10–100\ \text{kV} onto a target of tungsten (high melting point, high atomic number) embedded at about 45^{\circ} in a massive copper anode. The abrupt stopping of the electrons produces X-rays, which leave through a thin window. Over 99\% of the electron energy becomes heat, so the anode is cooled by circulating water or oil, or is rotated. Intensity (the number of X-ray photons per second) is controlled by the filament current, since that fixes how many electrons per second strike the target. Quality (the penetrating power, i.e. how short the wavelengths are) is controlled by the accelerating voltage: a higher voltage gives more energetic electrons, a shorter \lambda_{min}, and therefore "harder", more penetrating X-rays. The two controls are independent, which is exactly what a radiographer needs.

(b) Continuous spectrum: produced when incident electrons are decelerated in the electric field of the target nuclei, each losing an arbitrary part of its energy. Since the fraction lost can be anything from nearly zero up to everything, all wavelengths above a sharp minimum are produced, in a smooth distribution. It depends only on the accelerating voltage. Characteristic spectrum: produced when an incident electron ejects an electron from an inner (K or L) shell of a target atom. An outer electron drops into the vacancy and emits a photon of energy equal to the difference between two sharply defined atomic levels, giving intense discrete lines (K_\alpha, K_\beta, L_\alpha, …) superposed on the continuous background. These depend only on the target material and are its fingerprint. Derivation of the limit. An electron accelerated through V has kinetic energy

KE = eV

In the most extreme collision, the electron is stopped completely in one step and all of its energy goes into a single photon. That is the largest photon energy possible, hence the highest frequency and shortest wavelength:

eV = h\nu_{max} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{min}}

\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}

(c) For V = 20\ \text{kV}:

\lambda_{min} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^{8}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times2.0\times10^{4}} = 6.22\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}

For V = 50\ \text{kV}:

\lambda_{min} = \frac{1.989\times10^{-25}}{1.6\times10^{-19}\times5.0\times10^{4}} = 2.49\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}

Comment. Raising the voltage by a factor of 2.5 shortens \lambda_{min} by the same factor 2.5, since \lambda_{min} \propto 1/V. The shorter the wavelength, the more penetrating ("harder") the radiation — 50\ \text{kV} X-rays will pass through thicker tissue and denser bone than 20\ \text{kV} ones. Note also that this limit is independent of the target metal; only the characteristic lines depend on that.

Radius and energy of the nth Bohr orbit

We want the size of the allowed orbits of the hydrogen atom and the energy of the electron in each, starting from only two facts: the electrostatic force holds the electron in its circle, and the angular momentum can take only certain values.

Setting up. A hydrogen atom has one electron, of mass m and charge -e, moving in a circle of radius r with speed v about a nucleus of charge +e. Take the nucleus to be fixed, since it is about 1836 times heavier. The potential energy is measured from zero at infinite separation.

Step 1 — write the force that holds the electron in the circle. The only force is the electrostatic attraction, and it must supply exactly the centripetal force:

\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{e^{2}}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}

Step 2 — multiply both sides by r. This gives a useful expression for mv^{2}, which we will need twice:

mv^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 3 — write Bohr's quantisation condition. Only orbits with angular momentum an integer multiple of h/2\pi are allowed:

mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}

Step 4 — make v the subject. Divide both sides by mr:

v = \frac{nh}{2\pi mr}

Step 5 — substitute this v into the result of Step 2.

m\left(\frac{nh}{2\pi mr}\right)^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 6 — square the bracket and cancel one m.

\frac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mr^{2}} = \frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 7 — multiply both sides by r^{2} and solve for r. One power of r survives on the right:

r_n = \frac{\varepsilon_0 n^{2}h^{2}}{\pi m e^{2}}

Step 8 — write the kinetic energy. Halve the result of Step 2:

KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 9 — write the potential energy. For charges +e and -e separated by r, with zero at infinity, the potential energy is negative:

PE = -\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 10 — add them to get the total energy.

E = \frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}-\frac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = -\frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}

Step 11 — put in the value of r from Step 7.

E_n = -\frac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{\pi me^{2}}{\varepsilon_0n^{2}h^{2}}

Step 12 — collect the constants. The \pi cancels and the two e^{2} terms combine:

E_n = -\frac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}n^{2}}

Result.

r_n = \frac{\varepsilon_0 n^{2}h^{2}}{\pi m e^{2}} = 0.53\,n^{2}\ \text{Å}

E_n = -\frac{me^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{n^{2}} = -\frac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}

What it means. The radius grows as n^{2}, so the orbits get rapidly further apart: 0.53, 2.12, 4.77\ \text{Å} and so on. The smallest orbit, n = 1, is the Bohr radius, and it sets the size of the hydrogen atom — the atom cannot collapse because there is no orbit below it. The energy is negative, meaning the electron is bound; it rises towards zero as n increases, and the levels crowd together near the top. Taking the difference of two levels and using h\nu = E_i-E_f gives 1/\lambda = R\left(1/n_f^{2}-1/n_i^{2}\right) with R = me^{4}/8\varepsilon_0^{2}h^{3}c, and the value of R calculated from these constants alone agrees with the measured Rydberg constant 1.097\times10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}. That agreement, from a theory with no adjustable parameter, is why Bohr's model was accepted at once.

Conditions. The atom must have only one electron (hydrogen, \text{He}^{+}, \text{Li}^{2+}, for which e^{2} becomes Ze^{2} and E_n = -13.6Z^{2}/n^{2}); the nucleus is assumed infinitely heavy, and allowing for its motion changes the result by about 1 part in 2000; the speeds are taken as non-relativistic; and the whole picture of a definite orbit is, strictly, inconsistent with the uncertainty principle — it happens to give the right energies for one-electron atoms and fails for everything else.

Examiner's note — Quantization of energy

Almost every question here starts from the same two lines — the force equation and mvr = nh/2\pi — so write them both down even if the question seems to ask for something else. Keep the two proportionalities straight: r \propto n^{2} but E \propto -1/n^{2}. When you use Rydberg's formula, the smaller quantum number is always n_f and goes first inside the bracket; getting them the wrong way round gives a negative wavelength. The shortcut \lambda(\text{nm}) = 1242/E(\text{eV}) converts between the two halves of this unit in one step and makes checking easy. For X-rays, remember that \lambda_{min} depends only on the voltage while the characteristic lines depend only on the target; questions frequently test exactly that distinction.

Nature Helium nucleus ^{4}_{2}\text{He} Fast electron Electromagnetic wave (photon)
Charge +2e -e Zero
Mass 4\ \text{u} 1/1836\ \text{u} Zero rest mass

Penetrating power and ionising power always run opposite to each other: a heavily ionising particle spends its energy quickly and so does not get far.

(b) The \beta-particle, by a very large margin. The radius of the path is r = mv/qB, so the deflection is greatest for the smallest m/q. A \beta-particle has a mass about 7300 times smaller than an \alpha-particle and half the charge magnitude, so its m/q is smaller by a factor of about 3670 and it curves far more sharply. The \gamma-ray, being uncharged, is not deflected at all.

2. (a) Laws of radioactive disintegration. (i) Radioactivity is a spontaneous nuclear process, unaffected by temperature, pressure, chemical combination or any other physical condition — it is a property of the nucleus alone. (ii) The disintegration of a particular nucleus is entirely random; it is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next or when a given one will decay, and the process obeys only statistical laws. (iii) The rate of disintegration at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant:

-\frac{dN}{dt} \propto N \;\Rightarrow\; -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N

(iv) In each disintegration one \alpha or one \beta particle is emitted, never both together, and \gamma-radiation accompanies them when the daughter nucleus is left excited.

(b) \alpha-decay (Soddy-Fajans displacement law): the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2, so the daughter is two places to the left in the periodic table:

^{A}_{Z}X \longrightarrow\ ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}

Example: ^{238}_{92}\text{U} \longrightarrow\ ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}. \beta^{-}-decay: a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton and an electron, which is ejected; the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number increases by one, so the daughter is one place to the right:

^{A}_{Z}X \longrightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + ^{0}_{-1}e

Example: ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \longrightarrow\ ^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + ^{0}_{-1}e. \gamma-emission changes neither A nor Z; it only removes excess excitation energy.

3. (a) See the derivation box below. In outline: the third law of disintegration gives -dN/dt = \lambda N; separating the variables gives dN/N = -\lambda\,dt; integrating from N_0 at t = 0 to N at time t gives \ln(N/N_0) = -\lambda t; and taking exponentials,

N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}

(b) The decay constant \lambda is the constant of proportionality in -dN/dt = \lambda N: it is the fraction of the undecayed nuclei that decay per unit time, or equivalently the probability per unit time that any one nucleus will decay. Its unit is \text{s}^{-1}. A large \lambda means a rapidly decaying (short-lived) nuclide. From the exponential law, \lambda is also the reciprocal of the time in which the number falls to 1/e of its value.

4. (a) Half-life T_{1/2} is the time in which half the nuclei originally present have decayed, so that N = N_0/2. Mean life \tau is the average lifetime of all the nuclei in the sample, from formation to decay. Putting N = N_0/2 at t = T_{1/2} in N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}:

\frac{N_0}{2} = N_0e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \;\Rightarrow\; e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} = \frac{1}{2}

Taking natural logarithms of both sides,

-\lambda T_{1/2} = \ln\frac{1}{2} = -\ln2

T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}

(b) The mean life is the total lifetime of all the nuclei divided by their number. A nucleus that decays between t and t+dt has lived a time t, and the number doing so is \lambda N_0e^{-\lambda t}dt. Hence

\tau = \frac{1}{N_0}\int_0^{\infty}t\,\lambda N_0e^{-\lambda t}dt = \lambda\int_0^{\infty}te^{-\lambda t}dt

The standard integral \int_0^{\infty}te^{-\lambda t}dt = 1/\lambda^{2}, so

\tau = \lambda\cdot\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}} = \frac{1}{\lambda}

Combining with T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda,

\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{T_{1/2}}{0.693} = 1.44\,T_{1/2}

The mean life is always longer than the half-life, because the few very long-lived nuclei pull the average up.

5. (a) Activity is proportional to N, so the sample falls to 1/16 of its number.

\frac{1}{16} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n} \;\Rightarrow\; n = 4 \text{ half-lives}

T_{1/2} = \frac{80}{4} = 20\ \text{minutes}

\lambda = \frac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{20\times60} = 5.78\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}

(b) A further 40 minutes is two more half-lives, so the fraction remaining falls by a further factor of 2^{2} = 4:

\frac{N}{N_0} = \frac{1}{16}\times\frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{64}

(equivalently, 6 half-lives in total in 120 minutes, and (1/2)^{6} = 1/64).

A = -\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}

Its SI unit is the becquerel (Bq), one disintegration per second. The older unit is the curie (Ci), 1\ \text{Ci} = 3.7\times10^{10}\ \text{Bq}, originally the activity of one gram of radium. The rutherford (10^{6}\ \text{Bq}) is also occasionally met.

(b)

\lambda = \frac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{20\times60} = 5.78\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}

A = \lambda N = 5.78\times10^{-4}\times1.0\times10^{18}

7. (a) Construction. A Geiger-Müller tube is a hollow metal cylinder, or a glass tube with a conducting inner coating, which serves as the cathode. Along its axis runs a fine tungsten wire, the anode, insulated from the cylinder and ending in a small bead to avoid a point discharge. The tube is filled with an inert gas such as argon at low pressure (about 10\ \text{cm} of mercury) together with a small amount of a quenching vapour such as bromine or ethyl alcohol. One end is closed by a thin mica window through which \alpha and \beta particles can enter. A potential difference of about 400\ \text{V} is applied between the wire and the cylinder through a high resistance R of a few megohms. Working. The applied voltage is set just below the value at which the gas would break down on its own. When an ionising particle enters, it produces a few ion pairs. The strong radial field near the thin wire accelerates the freed electrons so violently that they ionise further atoms, and those ionise still more: an avalanche spreads along the whole length of the wire. A large pulse of current flows momentarily, producing a voltage pulse across R, which is amplified and fed to a scaler or ratemeter and counted. The quenching vapour absorbs the ultraviolet photons and neutralises the positive ions before they can strike the cathode and start a spurious second discharge, so the tube recovers and is ready for the next particle.

(b) The dead time is the short interval, typically 100–200\ \mu\text{s}, immediately after a count, during which the slow positive-ion sheath around the wire has reduced the field so much that a second particle entering the tube cannot produce a countable avalanche. Any particle arriving during this time is missed, so at high count rates the observed rate is lower than the true rate and a dead-time correction must be applied.

8. (a) Carbon dating. Cosmic-ray neutrons striking nitrogen in the upper atmosphere continuously produce the radioactive isotope ^{14}_{6}\text{C}, which mixes with ordinary carbon as carbon dioxide. Because production and decay have been in balance for a long time, the ratio of ^{14}\text{C} to ^{12}\text{C} in the atmosphere is essentially constant. A living plant or animal constantly exchanges carbon with its surroundings, so it carries this same ratio and shows a constant ^{14}\text{C} activity of about 15 disintegrations per minute per gram of carbon. The moment the organism dies, the exchange stops. No new ^{14}\text{C} enters, and the ^{14}\text{C} already there decays with a half-life of 5730 years. Measuring the residual activity per gram of carbon and comparing it with that of living material gives the number of half-lives that have passed, and hence the age, from A = A_0e^{-\lambda t}. The method is reliable for objects between about 500 and 50\,000 years old — beyond that too little ^{14}\text{C} remains to measure. It is used to date wood, charcoal, bone, cloth and manuscripts.

(b) 25\% = 1/4 = (1/2)^{2}, so exactly two half-lives have elapsed:

t = 2\times5730 = 11\,460\ \text{years}

Check with the formula: \lambda = 0.693/5730 = 1.21\times10^{-4}\ \text{yr}^{-1}, and t = \ln(4)/\lambda = 1.386/1.21\times10^{-4} = 1.15\times10^{4} years. ✓

9. (a) Mass defect \Delta m is the difference between the sum of the masses of the free, separate nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus they form:

\Delta m = \left[Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n\right] - M_{nucleus}

The missing mass has been converted into the energy released when the nucleus was assembled. Binding energy is the corresponding energy, BE = \Delta m\,c^{2} — the energy that would have to be supplied to pull the nucleus completely apart into free nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon is BE/A; it measures the stability of the nucleus and peaks at about 8.8\ \text{MeV} near iron (A \approx 56), which is why heavy nuclei release energy by fission and light ones by fusion.

(b)

BE = \Delta m\times931.5 = 0.0304\times931.5 = 28.3\ \text{MeV}

\frac{BE}{A} = \frac{28.3}{4} = 7.08\ \text{MeV per nucleon}

This is unusually high for such a light nucleus, which is why the \alpha-particle is exceptionally stable and why heavy nuclei emit it whole rather than emitting separate nucleons.

10. (a) Medical uses. (i) Diagnosis with tracers: a small quantity of a short-lived isotope is given to the patient and its progress followed with a detector — ^{131}\text{I} for the thyroid, ^{99m}\text{Tc} for bone, kidney and heart scans, ^{24}\text{Na} to trace blood circulation and find clots. (ii) Radiotherapy: a beam of \gamma-rays from a ^{60}\text{Co} source, or an implanted source, is directed at a tumour to destroy the rapidly dividing cancer cells, which are more sensitive to radiation than normal tissue. (iii) Sterilisation: \gamma-radiation sterilises syringes, dressings, sutures and surgical instruments in their sealed packets, without heat. (iv) Radiography with X-rays, and the preservation of food from spoilage.

(b) Hazards. (i) Somatic damage — radiation ionises the molecules of living cells; large doses cause radiation sickness, burns, loss of hair, damage to the blood-forming tissue and, after long exposure, leukaemia and other cancers. (ii) Genetic damage — ionisation in the reproductive cells alters the DNA, and the resulting mutations are passed to later generations. Damage is cumulative, and there is no dose so small that it is certainly harmless. Precautions. (i) Keep the source at the greatest possible distance and handle it with long tongs, never with bare hands, since the dose falls as the inverse square of the distance. (ii) Store sources in thick lead containers and work behind lead or concrete shielding, with lead aprons for staff. (iii) Minimise the time of exposure and wear a film badge or dosimeter so that the accumulated dose is monitored against the permitted limit. (iv) Use the shortest-lived isotope that will do the job, and dispose of radioactive waste properly.
