Model answers — long

1. (a) Laws: radioactivity is a spontaneous nuclear process unaffected by physical or chemical conditions; the decay of an individual nucleus is completely random; and the rate of decay at any instant is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present. The derivation from the third law is in the box below; the result is

N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}

(b) Half-life T_{1/2} is the time for half the nuclei present to decay; mean life \tau is the average life of all the nuclei. Setting N = N_0/2 at t = T_{1/2}:

\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \;\Rightarrow\; \ln\frac{1}{2} = -\lambda T_{1/2}

T_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}

For the mean life, the number decaying between t and t+dt is \lambda N_0e^{-\lambda t}dt and each such nucleus lived a time t, so

\tau = \frac{1}{N_0}\int_0^{\infty}\lambda N_0te^{-\lambda t}dt = \lambda\cdot\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}} = \frac{1}{\lambda}

Hence \tau = T_{1/2}/0.693 = 1.44\,T_{1/2}: the mean life exceeds the half-life.

(c)

\frac{1}{16} = \left(\frac12\right)^{4} \;\Rightarrow\; 4\ \text{half-lives in }80\ \text{min} \;\Rightarrow\; T_{1/2} = 20\ \text{min}

\lambda = \frac{0.693}{20\times60} = 5.78\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}

In 120 minutes there are 120/20 = 6 half-lives, so

\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac12\right)^{6} = \frac{1}{64} = 1.56\%

2. (a) The comparison table is in short answer 1(a): \alpha is a helium nucleus, charge +2e, mass 4\ \text{u}, least penetrating but most ionising; \beta is a fast electron, charge -e, tiny mass, moderately penetrating and moderately ionising; \gamma is an uncharged, massless photon, most penetrating and least ionising. In a magnetic field \alpha and \beta bend in opposite directions (\beta far more sharply, because of its very small m/q) while \gamma goes straight through. Displacement laws.

^{A}_{Z}X \longrightarrow\ ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^{4}_{2}\text{He} \quad (\alpha)

Example: ^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \longrightarrow\ ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}.

^{A}_{Z}X \longrightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z+1}Y + ^{0}_{-1}e \quad (\beta^{-})

Example: ^{14}_{6}\text{C} \longrightarrow\ ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}e. In \alpha-decay the element moves two places left in the periodic table; in \beta-decay, one place right. \gamma-emission changes neither A nor Z and simply carries away excitation energy from the daughter nucleus.

(b) Construction and working: as described in short answer 7(a). Metal cylinder (cathode) with a fine axial tungsten wire (anode), inert gas at low pressure with a quenching vapour, thin mica window, about 400\ \text{V} applied through a few megohms. An entering ionising particle produces a few ion pairs; the intense radial field near the thin wire accelerates the electrons enough to cause a self-sustaining avalanche; the resulting current pulse develops a voltage across the resistor, which is amplified and counted. The quenching vapour stops the discharge so the tube is ready for the next particle.

(c) Dead time is the interval of 100–200\ \mu\text{s} after each count during which the sluggish positive-ion sheath near the wire suppresses the field, so a second particle produces no countable pulse. Counts arriving in this interval are lost, and at high rates a correction must be made to obtain the true count rate.

3. (a) Carbon dating. ^{14}\text{C} is produced continuously in the upper atmosphere by cosmic-ray neutrons acting on nitrogen, and it decays with a half-life of 5730 years, so its proportion in atmospheric carbon dioxide has remained nearly constant. Living things exchange carbon with their surroundings and therefore carry the same ^{14}\text{C}:{^{12}\text{C}} ratio, giving an activity of about 15 counts per minute per gram of carbon. At death the exchange stops and the ^{14}\text{C} decays without replacement, so the activity falls exponentially. Measuring the present activity per gram and comparing it with the living value gives t from A = A_0e^{-\lambda t}. Range and limitations: usable from about 500 to about 50\,000 years — after roughly 10 half-lives too little ^{14}\text{C} is left to measure reliably. It works only on once-living material (wood, charcoal, bone, cloth, seeds), not on stone or metal. It assumes the atmospheric ^{14}\text{C} level has been constant, which is not exactly true (it has been disturbed by volcanic activity, by the burning of fossil fuel and by nuclear weapons testing), so calibration curves from tree rings are used. Contamination of the sample by modern carbon makes it appear too young.

(b) Activity A = \lambda N is the number of disintegrations per second; unit the becquerel. Mass defect \Delta m = [Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n] - M_{nucleus} is the mass that disappears when free nucleons combine. Binding energy per nucleon = \Delta m\,c^{2}/A is the energy needed per nucleon to break the nucleus into its separate parts; it is a direct measure of stability and is greatest (\approx8.8\ \text{MeV}) for nuclei near iron.

(c) Age of the relic. 25\% is (1/2)^{2}, so two half-lives:

t = 2\times5730 = 1.15\times10^{4}\ \text{years}

Activity of the source.

\lambda = \frac{0.693}{20\times60} = 5.78\times10^{-4}\ \text{s}^{-1}

A = \lambda N = 5.78\times10^{-4}\times1.0\times10^{18} = 5.8\times10^{14}\ \text{Bq}

(That is about 1.6\times10^{4} curie — a ferociously hot source, which is why short-lived tracers are used in only microgram quantities.)

The law of radioactive decay, N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}

We start from the single experimental fact that the decay rate is proportional to how much undecayed material is left, and reach the exponential law and the half-life.

Setting up. A sample contains N_0 undecayed nuclei at time t = 0 and N at a later time t. Each nucleus decays independently and at random, but the chance that any one nucleus decays in the next second is a fixed number \lambda, characteristic of the nuclide and unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical state.

Step 1 — write the number expected to decay in a short time dt. If each of the N nuclei has a probability \lambda\,dt of decaying, the expected number of decays is N\lambda\,dt. Since N is falling, the change dN is negative:

-dN = \lambda N\,dt

Step 2 — write it as a rate. Divide both sides by dt:

-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N

Step 3 — separate the variables. Put everything containing N on one side and everything containing t on the other. Divide both sides by N and multiply by dt:

\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt

Step 4 — integrate both sides between the corresponding limits. At t = 0 the number is N_0; at time t it is N:

\int_{N_0}^{N}\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\int_0^{t}dt

Step 5 — carry out the two integrations. The integral of 1/N is \ln N, and the integral of dt is t:

\left[\ln N\right]_{N_0}^{N} = -\lambda\left[t\right]_0^{t}

Step 6 — put in the limits.

\ln N - \ln N_0 = -\lambda t

Step 7 — combine the two logarithms. The difference of two logarithms is the logarithm of the quotient:

\ln\frac{N}{N_0} = -\lambda t

Step 8 — undo the logarithm. Raise e to the power of each side:

\frac{N}{N_0} = e^{-\lambda t}

Step 9 — multiply through by N_0.

N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}

Step 10 — find the half-life. By definition N = N_0/2 when t = T_{1/2}:

\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}

Step 11 — take logarithms of both sides.

-\ln 2 = -\lambda T_{1/2}

Result.

N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}, \qquad A = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}

T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}, \qquad \tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}

What it means. The number left falls by the same factor in every equal interval of time — a half in every half-life, giving 100\%, 50\%, 25\%, 12.5\% and so on (Figure 21). It never reaches zero exactly, which is why we speak of a half-life rather than a "total life". Because the activity A = \lambda N is proportional to N, activity obeys exactly the same exponential law, which is what makes the law testable: one counts clicks, not atoms. Taking logarithms of the result gives \ln N = \ln N_0 - \lambda t, so a graph of \ln A against t is a straight line of slope -\lambda — the standard laboratory method of measuring a half-life. Note that \lambda is fixed by the nucleus alone: an old nucleus is no more likely to decay than a newly formed one, so radioactive nuclei do not "age".

Conditions. The sample must contain a large number of nuclei, since the law is statistical and fluctuates badly when only a few are left; the daughter product must be stable, or its own decay must be treated separately; and \lambda must be constant, which is true to extremely high accuracy because the process is nuclear and the nucleus is shielded from all chemical and thermal influence.

Examiner's note — Radioactivity and nuclear reaction

Most numericals here need no calculator at all: express the surviving fraction as a power of \tfrac12, count the half-lives, and stop. Use \lambda = 0.693/T_{1/2} only when the question asks for \lambda or the activity, and keep T_{1/2} in seconds when a becquerel answer is wanted — forgetting the \times60 is the commonest slip in this unit. In the decay-law derivation, show the separation of variables and both limits of integration; jumping straight to the exponential loses half the marks. Learn the displacement laws as movements in the periodic table (\alpha: two places left; \beta: one place right), and remember that penetrating power and ionising power always run in opposite order.

Model answers — short (1–5)

1. (a) Body waves travel through the interior of the Earth, spreading out in three dimensions from the focus; they are the P- and S-waves, they are the fastest and arrive first at a seismograph, and their amplitude falls off quickly with distance. Surface waves travel along or near the Earth's surface, like ripples on water; they are the Rayleigh and Love waves, they are slower and arrive last, but they have much larger amplitudes and decay more slowly with distance, so they do most of the damage.

(b)

P-wave (primary) S-wave (secondary)
Nature Longitudinal — particles vibrate along the direction of travel (compressions and rarefactions) Transverse — particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel
Speed in crust 6–8\ \text{km s}^{-1} — the fastest, so recorded first 3.5–4.5\ \text{km s}^{-1}, about 0.6 times the P-speed
Media Travels through solids, liquids and gases Travels through solids only
Damage Small Larger than P

The reason for the difference in media is that a transverse wave needs a shear restoring force, and liquids and gases have no rigidity, so they cannot support shear.

2. (a) Rayleigh waves travel along the free surface of the ground and make each particle move in a vertical ellipse, rolling backwards relative to the direction of propagation — the motion is like that of a water wave, a combination of longitudinal and vertical transverse displacement. They are the slowest seismic waves (about 0.9 times the S-speed) and usually have the largest amplitude of all; the visible "rolling" of the ground in a strong earthquake is a Rayleigh wave. Love waves are surface waves in which the particles move horizontally, side to side, at right angles to the direction of travel and parallel to the surface, with no vertical motion at all. They exist only when a low-velocity surface layer overlies a faster substratum, in which the shear waves are trapped and guided. They travel slightly faster than Rayleigh waves and are particularly destructive to the foundations of buildings, which resist vertical loads well but horizontal shaking badly.

(b) Three reasons. (i) Amplitude. Surface waves are confined to a thin layer near the surface, so their energy is spread over an area rather than a volume; their amplitude therefore falls off only as 1/\sqrt{r} instead of the 1/r of body waves, and they arrive still large at great distances. (ii) Low frequency and long duration. They have longer periods and go on shaking for many cycles, so they can drive tall buildings into resonance — a building with a natural period matching the wave suffers enormous amplitudes. (iii) Horizontal motion. Love waves shake the ground sideways, and ordinary buildings are far weaker against horizontal forces than vertical ones. Arriving last is no protection, because the damage is done by the amplitude, not the arrival order.

3. (a) P-waves travel faster than S-waves, so the gap between their arrivals grows steadily with distance from the epicentre — the further away the station, the bigger the S-P time difference. Each seismograph station measures this difference and converts it into a distance d using the known speeds (or a standard travel-time curve):

\frac{d}{v_s}-\frac{d}{v_p} = \Delta t \;\Rightarrow\; d = \frac{\Delta t}{\dfrac{1}{v_s}-\dfrac{1}{v_p}}

This gives the distance but not the direction, so the station can only say that the epicentre lies somewhere on a circle of radius d drawn round it on the map. Repeating the measurement at a second station gives a second circle, which cuts the first at two points, and a third station resolves the ambiguity: the single point where all three circles intersect is the epicentre. This method is called triangulation.

(b)

d = \frac{\Delta t}{\dfrac{1}{v_s}-\dfrac{1}{v_p}} = \frac{60}{\dfrac{1}{4.0}-\dfrac{1}{8.0}} = \frac{60}{0.125}

d = 480\ \text{km}

Check: t_P = 480/8.0 = 60\ \text{s} and t_S = 480/4.0 = 120\ \text{s}, a difference of exactly 60\ \text{s}. ✓

4. (a) The Gorkha earthquake struck on 25 April 2015 at about 11{:}56 local time. Its moment magnitude was 7.8, and its epicentre was near Barpak in Gorkha district, roughly 80\ \text{km} north-west of Kathmandu, at a shallow focal depth of about 15\ \text{km}. A major aftershock of magnitude 7.3 followed on 12 May 2015 near Dolakha, and thousands of smaller aftershocks continued for months. Nearly 9000 people died, about 22\,000 were injured, and huge numbers of houses and many historic monuments in the Kathmandu valley were destroyed. Cause. Nepal lies on the collision boundary where the Indian plate is being driven northward beneath the Eurasian plate at about 45\ \text{mm} per year. Friction locks the two plates along the Main Frontal Thrust, strain energy accumulates in the rock for centuries, and when the stress exceeds the strength of the rock the fault slips suddenly, releasing the stored elastic energy as seismic waves. In 2015 a section of the fault about 120\ \text{km} long slipped by several metres. The shallow focus and the soft sediments of the Kathmandu valley, which amplified the long-period surface waves, made the shaking especially destructive.

(b) It tells us that the outer core is liquid. S-waves are transverse, and a transverse wave needs a shear (rigidity) restoring force. Liquids have no rigidity — they flow rather than resist a shearing stress — so they cannot transmit an S-wave. The observation that no S-waves at all arrive in the shadow zone beyond about 103^{\circ} from the epicentre, while P-waves do arrive (refracted, and delayed), is the classic evidence that the outer core is molten. The later discovery that P-waves are refracted again at a deeper boundary showed that the inner core is solid.

5. (a) Gravitational waves are ripples in the curvature of space-time itself, predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity in 1916 and produced whenever mass is accelerated unsymmetrically — for example by two neutron stars or black holes spiralling round each other, or by an asymmetric supernova. Properties: (i) they travel at the speed of light; (ii) they are transverse — they stretch space in one direction while squeezing it in the perpendicular direction, alternately, as they pass; (iii) they interact with matter extraordinarily weakly, so they pass through the Earth almost undisturbed and can bring information from regions that light cannot escape; (iv) their amplitude falls off as 1/r, and the strain they produce at the Earth is of order 10^{-21}; (v) they carry energy away from the source, which is why a binary pulsar's orbit slowly shrinks — the indirect evidence for which Hulse and Taylor won the Nobel Prize in 1993.

(b) They were first detected directly on 14 September 2015 by the two LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) detectors at Hanford and Livingston in the United States; the discovery was announced on 11 February 2016 and the event is named GW150914. The signal came from the merger of two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses, about 1.3 billion light years away, which combined into a single black hole of about 62 solar masses — roughly three solar masses of material being converted into the energy of gravitational waves in a fraction of a second. The Nobel Prize in Physics for 2017 went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne for this work.

Model answers — short (6–9)

6. (a) LIGO is a giant Michelson interferometer. A powerful laser beam is split by a half-silvered mirror into two beams that travel down two evacuated arms set at right angles, each 4\ \text{km} long, reflect from mirrors at the far ends (in practice bouncing back and forth hundreds of times in optical cavities to lengthen the effective path), and return to recombine at the detector. The arms are adjusted so that the two returning beams normally interfere destructively and the detector sees darkness. A passing gravitational wave is transverse: it stretches one arm while shrinking the other, then reverses. The two light paths are therefore no longer equal, the path difference changes, and the interference pattern shifts, so a flicker of light appears at the previously dark output. The pattern of that flicker with time is a direct recording of the wave. Two detectors thousands of kilometres apart are used, so that a real signal must appear at both with the correct light-travel delay; local disturbances affect only one.

(b) Because the effect is unimaginably small. A strong astronomical source produces a strain of only about h \approx 10^{-21}, so in a 4\ \text{km} arm the change in length is

\Delta L = hL \approx 10^{-21}\times4\times10^{3} = 4\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}

which is about one thousandth of the diameter of a proton. Measuring this requires the mirrors to be suspended in a near-perfect vacuum on elaborate multi-stage isolation systems, cooled and shielded, and protected from seismic tremors, passing traffic, ocean waves, thermal vibration of the mirror atoms and even the random arrival of individual photons. Gravity is by far the weakest of the four fundamental interactions, which is exactly why gravitational waves are so penetrating and so hard to catch.

7. (a) Nanotechnology is the study, design, production and application of structures, devices and systems by controlling the shape and size of matter at the scale of a few nanometres. A nanometre is 10^{-9}\ \text{m}, about the length of ten hydrogen atoms in a row. The nanoscale is conventionally the range 1 to 100\ \text{nm} — big enough to contain hundreds or thousands of atoms, small enough that the ordinary bulk properties of the material no longer apply.

(b) Two effects take over at this size. (i) The surface-to-volume ratio becomes enormous. For a cube of side a this ratio is 6/a, so shrinking the cube from 1\ \text{cm} to 1\ \text{nm} increases it ten million times. A very large fraction of the atoms are then surface atoms, with unsatisfied bonds, so the material becomes far more chemically reactive, a far better catalyst, and melts at a much lower temperature than the bulk. (ii) Quantum confinement. When a particle is smaller than the natural wavelength of its electrons, the electron energy levels are no longer continuous bands but become discrete, and their spacing depends on the size of the particle. So the optical and electrical properties can be tuned by size alone: cadmium selenide quantum dots of different diameters, made of exactly the same substance, fluoresce in different colours. Gold, which is yellow and inert in bulk, is red in 10\ \text{nm} particles and is an excellent catalyst.

8. (a) Applications. (i) Medicine: targeted drug delivery, in which a drug is carried in a nanoparticle that releases it only at a tumour, reducing side effects; nanoparticle contrast agents for imaging; and nanoscale biosensors for early diagnosis. (ii) Electronics: transistors with features a few nanometres across, giving faster and denser integrated circuits; memory devices; carbon nanotubes and graphene for flexible, transparent conductors. (iii) Materials: carbon-nanotube composites that are exceptionally strong and light for sports equipment and aircraft; scratch-resistant, self-cleaning and water-repellent coatings; stain-resistant fabrics; nano-silver antibacterial coatings. (iv) Energy and environment: more efficient solar cells, better battery and fuel-cell electrodes, nano-catalysts, and membranes and nano-filters for purifying water. (v) Cosmetics: zinc oxide and titanium dioxide nanoparticles in sunscreens, which block ultraviolet but are transparent.

(b) Risks. (i) Health. Nanoparticles are small enough to pass through the lungs into the bloodstream and even to cross the blood-brain barrier, and their large reactive surface may damage cells; the long-term effects of inhaling them are not yet known, and some nanotubes behave in the lungs somewhat like asbestos fibres. (ii) Environment. They are difficult to detect, filter or clean up once released, and may accumulate in soil, water and living organisms; nano-silver released from fabrics can harm useful bacteria in sewage treatment. (iii) Other concerns are the misuse of invisible nano-sensors for surveillance, possible military applications, and the economic disruption caused if nano-materials replace natural raw materials on which poor countries depend.

9. (a) The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle of the Standard Model — the quantum, or particle-like excitation, of the Higgs field. The Higgs field is supposed to fill all of space uniformly, even in a perfect vacuum. Particles that interact with this field are slowed by it, and this resistance to acceleration is exactly what we call mass: the more strongly a particle couples to the Higgs field, the more massive it is, while the photon, which does not couple at all, remains massless. The mechanism (proposed independently in 1964 by Higgs, by Englert and Brout, and by others) is what allows the W and Z bosons to be heavy while the photon is massless, even though the electromagnetic and weak interactions are otherwise unified. Without it the Standard Model would predict that electrons and quarks have no mass, and atoms could not exist. Its mass is about 125\ \text{GeV}/c^{2}, some 133 times that of a proton; it has zero charge and zero spin, the only known fundamental scalar particle, and it decays almost instantly.

(b) It was discovered at CERN, near Geneva, at the Large Hadron Collider, and announced on 4 July 2012 by the two independent experiments ATLAS and CMS. Protons were accelerated in opposite directions round the 27\ \text{km} ring and made to collide at very high energy; occasionally a collision produced a Higgs boson, which decayed at once into particles such as two photons or four leptons. The Higgs itself was never seen — it was inferred from a small statistical excess of such decay events at a common reconstructed mass of about 125\ \text{GeV}, which rose above the background as more and more collisions were recorded. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013.

1. (a)

Wave Type Speed Medium Damage
P (primary) Body, longitudinal 6–8\ \text{km s}^{-1}, fastest Solid, liquid and gas Least
S (secondary) Body, transverse 3.5–4.5\ \text{km s}^{-1} Solids only Moderate

The order of arrival at a seismograph is therefore P, then S, then the surface waves (Figure 22). Body waves spread through a volume, so their amplitude falls as 1/r; surface waves are confined to a thin layer and fall only as 1/\sqrt{r}, which is why they still dominate the record at great distances and cause most of the destruction.

(b) Locating the epicentre. Since P is faster than S, the S-P arrival-time difference grows with distance. Each station converts its measured \Delta t into a distance,

d = \frac{\Delta t}{\dfrac{1}{v_S}-\dfrac{1}{v_P}}

and draws a circle of that radius round itself on the map. One station gives a circle, two give two intersection points, and a third station picks out the single common point — the epicentre. This is triangulation. The shadow zone. Beyond about 103^{\circ} of arc from the epicentre, no S-waves are received anywhere, and between about 103^{\circ} and 142^{\circ} no direct P-waves arrive either. The complete absence of S-waves shows that they have met a layer with no rigidity, so the outer core must be liquid; the refraction and delay of the P-waves that do get through gives the depth of that boundary (2900\ \text{km}), and a further refraction inside it reveals a solid inner core. Nearly everything we know about the deep interior of the Earth comes from such observations, since no borehole reaches even through the crust.

(c)

d = \frac{\Delta t}{\dfrac{1}{v_S}-\dfrac{1}{v_P}} = \frac{60}{\dfrac{1}{4.0}-\dfrac{1}{8.0}} = \frac{60}{0.250-0.125}

d = \frac{60}{0.125} = 480\ \text{km}

Check: t_P = 480/8.0 = 60\ \text{s}, t_S = 480/4.0 = 120\ \text{s}, difference 60\ \text{s}. ✓

2. (a) Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space-time, predicted by Einstein in 1916, radiated whenever mass undergoes unsymmetrical acceleration. Properties: they travel at the speed of light; they are transverse, stretching space along one axis while compressing it along the perpendicular axis and then reversing; they interact with matter extremely weakly, so they pass through the Earth essentially unchanged and carry information out of regions from which no light can escape; their amplitude falls as 1/r; and they carry energy away from their source, gradually shrinking the orbits of binary stars. How LIGO detects them. LIGO is a Michelson interferometer with two evacuated arms 4\ \text{km} long at right angles. Laser light is split between the arms, reflected from mirrors at the far ends (many times, in resonant cavities, to increase the effective path length) and recombined. The instrument is set so that the recombined beams normally cancel and the output is dark. A passing gravitational wave lengthens one arm and shortens the other, changing the path difference; the interference is upset and light appears at the output, its variation with time tracing the waveform. Two widely separated detectors must record the same signal, with the right light-travel delay between them, before it is accepted.

(b) The difficulty is the size of the effect. With a strain h = 10^{-21} and L = 4\ \text{km},

\Delta L = hL = 10^{-21}\times4\times10^{3} = 4\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}

which is about 1/1000 of the diameter of a proton, and roughly 10^{-13} of the wavelength of the laser light used to measure it. Everything conspires against the measurement: ground tremors, traffic, ocean waves, thermal jiggling of the atoms in the mirrors, residual gas molecules in the tube and the statistical noise of the photons themselves are all far larger. LIGO therefore uses multi-stage pendulum suspensions, an ultra-high vacuum, very high laser power, mirrors of exceptional quality, and coincidence between two detectors 3000\ \text{km} apart. Gravity is about 10^{36} times weaker than the electromagnetic force, which is both why the waves are so penetrating and why they are so nearly undetectable.

(c) The first direct detection, GW150914, was made on 14 September 2015 by both LIGO detectors and announced on 11 February 2016. The source was the merger of two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses at a distance of about 1.3 billion light years; the final black hole had about 62 solar masses, so roughly three solar masses were radiated away as gravitational waves in a few tenths of a second — briefly outshining, in this form of energy, all the stars in the observable universe. Significance: it was the first direct confirmation of a prediction Einstein made a century earlier; the first direct observation of black holes and of a black-hole merger; and the opening of gravitational-wave astronomy, an entirely new way of observing the universe that does not depend on light and can therefore probe the dark and the very early universe. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for it.

3. (a) Nanotechnology is the deliberate design, production and use of materials and devices whose structure is controlled at the scale of a few nanometres, where matter behaves differently from the bulk. A nanometre is 10^{-9}\ \text{m}; the nanoscale is from 1 to 100\ \text{nm}. Why matter behaves differently. Two reasons dominate. (i) Surface-to-volume ratio. For a cube of side a the ratio of surface area to volume is 6a^{2}/a^{3} = 6/a, which is inversely proportional to size. Going from a = 1\ \text{cm} to a = 1\ \text{nm} raises it from 600\ \text{m}^{-1} to 6\times10^{9}\ \text{m}^{-1} — ten million times greater. An enormous fraction of the atoms are then at the surface with unsatisfied bonds, so nanoparticles are far more reactive, are superb catalysts, and melt far below the bulk melting point. (ii) Quantum confinement. When the particle is comparable with the electron's de Broglie wavelength, the electrons are boxed in and their energy levels become discrete and size-dependent instead of forming continuous bands. The optical and electrical properties can then be tuned by changing the size alone — quantum dots of the same chemical substance fluoresce red, green or blue according to their diameter.

(b) Applications: targeted drug delivery and nanomedicine; nanoscale transistors, memory and graphene electronics; strong light composites and self-cleaning, scratch-resistant coatings; and efficient solar cells, better batteries and nano-membranes for water purification. (Others: sunscreens, antibacterial silver coatings, nano-sensors.) Risks: (i) health — particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs and to cross the blood-brain barrier, with unknown long-term effects and an asbestos-like hazard from some nanotubes; (ii) environment — they are hard to detect or remove once released, may accumulate in water, soil and living things, and may disturb useful micro-organisms.

(c) The Higgs boson is the quantum of the Higgs field, a field believed to fill the whole of space. Particles acquire mass by interacting with this field: the stronger the coupling, the greater the resistance to acceleration, and therefore the greater the mass; the photon does not couple and stays massless. This mechanism completes the Standard Model by explaining how the W and Z bosons of the weak interaction can be heavy while the photon is not. The particle has a mass of about 125\ \text{GeV}/c^{2} (about 133 proton masses), zero charge and zero spin. Discovery: at CERN's Large Hadron Collider near Geneva, announced on 4 July 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS experiments independently. Protons collided head-on at very high energy; a Higgs boson produced in a rare collision decayed immediately, and its existence was inferred from a statistical excess of decay products (two photons, or four leptons) clustering at a common mass near 125\ \text{GeV}. Higgs and Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize.

Examiner's note — Recent trends in physics

This unit rewards specific facts, not vague description. Fix in your memory: P longitudinal and fastest, S transverse and blocked by liquids (hence the liquid outer core), Rayleigh rolling and Love horizontal; Gorkha, 25 April 2015, magnitude 7.8, epicentre Barpak; LIGO, 14 September 2015, two black holes, strain 10^{-21}; nanoscale 1–100\ \text{nm}, with surface-to-volume ratio and quantum confinement as the two reasons for the new behaviour; Higgs boson, CERN, 4 July 2012, about 125\ \text{GeV}/c^{2}. Chapter summary

  • Sixty-four of the seventy-five marks are subjective. Group B carries 8\times5 = 40 and Group C 3\times8 = 24; the eleven multiple-choice marks of Group A cannot rescue a candidate who cannot write. Every question in this chapter is built to the real mark splits — 1+2+2, 2+3, 1+1+3 and 1+4 for the five-mark questions, and 2+2+2+2, 3+3+2 and 5+3 for the eight-mark ones.
  • The chapter covers all twenty-five CDC units in spine order, from Rotational dynamics to Recent trends in physics, with at least five short and two long questions in each, every one followed by a complete model answer written at the length an examiner expects to see in the answer book.
  • Every examinable derivation is worked step by step, either in a derivation box (energy in an inductor, the LCR impedance, Thomson's e/m, Einstein's photoelectric equation, the Bohr orbit) or inside the model answer itself: the moment of inertia of a rod, the vertical spring, Bernoulli's equation, Stokes' law, C_P-C_V = R, Carnot efficiency, the speed of a pulse in a fluid, pipes and strings, Doppler, fringe width, Brewster, the Wheatstone balance, the circular coil, Ampère's law and parallel conductors. Each gives one algebraic move per line, so the proof can be reproduced under examination pressure rather than recited.
  • Every numerical was recomputed before it was printed, and the answers are written out with units at each step. Where a result can be checked a second way — P = VI\cos\phi against I^{2}R, \beta against \alpha/(1-\alpha), a Bohr energy against a Rydberg wavelength — the check is shown, because writing it earns marks and catches slips.
  • A year tag such as (NEB 2081) marks a question that has actually been asked, in that year or in that model set. Untagged questions are new, but are built to the same pattern. Where several years carry the same tag, the topic is one that the board returns to almost every session and should be prepared first.
  • Twelve figures carry the parts of the answer that words cannot: the energy graphs of SHM, the isotherm and adiabat, the Otto and Carnot cycles, the stationary-wave patterns in pipes, the potentiometer circuit, the thermocouple curve, the hysteresis loop, the LCR phasor and resonance curve and the rectifier waveforms, with the remaining diagrams of the modern-physics units. In the examination, a clear labelled diagram is often worth two of the five marks on its own.
  • The units are not equally weighted. Magnetic field (9 h), Quantization of energy (8 h) and Fluid statics (9 h) are the largest, while Wave motion, Interference and Photons run to only two or three hours each — but the short units supply the opening parts of longer questions, so none can be skipped.
  • Read each Examiner's note. They record the mistakes that cost marks year after year: kelvin inside a square root, I as the reference phasor, the base current in microamperes, the smaller quantum number first in Rydberg's formula, and the habit of writing down the assumption before the algebra.
